stem: An interviewer asks you to type a `Button` that takes a required `label` string and an optional click handler that receives no arguments. Callers that omit `label` or pass a number should get a compile error. Which version meets every requirement under `strict`?

options.why: Props arrive as one object, so you type that object. `onClick?` makes the handler optional, and `label: string` rejects a missing or numeric label.
React calls a component with a single props object, not with positional arguments. `<Button label="Save" />` is rejected because the first parameter is typed `string`.
With no annotation, the destructured props are implicitly `any`. Under `strict` (`noImplicitAny`) this is a compile error, and even without it nothing would be checked.
`() => void | undefined` is a required function whose return type is `void | undefined`. The prop itself is not optional, so `<Button label="Save" />` fails.

explanation: A function component receives a single props object, so you type it with an object type and destructure it. Optional props use `?`. Interviewers asking this at the junior level want to see that you type the props object (not positional parameters), know where the `?` goes, and avoid leaving props as implicit `any`.

options.text: `any[]`; the error comes from `noImplicitAny` because the array has no element type
options.why: With `strictNullChecks` on, an empty array literal is inferred as `never[]`, not `any[]`. An `any[]` state would accept the strings.

options.text: `never[]`, so no string can ever be assigned to it
options.why: `useState` infers its state type from the initial value. `[]` is `never[]` under strict mode, so the setter only accepts `never[]`. Writing `useState<string[]>([])` fixes it.

options.text: `unknown[]`; strings must be narrowed before they can be stored
options.why: TypeScript never infers `unknown[]` from `[]`. And `unknown[]` would accept strings without narrowing.

options.text: `string[]`; the error is that `setItems` needs a callback form `prev => [...]`
options.why: The state is not `string[]`, and the setter accepts a plain value as well as an updater function.

explanation: `useState` infers the state type from its initial value. When that value does not describe the full type (an empty array, `null`, `undefined`), pass the type argument explicitly: `useState<string[]>([])`. This is one of the most common React-with-TypeScript mistakes interviewers ask about.

options.text: Inside the component, `size` has type `number`, because the default value removes `undefined`
options.why: A destructuring default replaces `undefined`, so TypeScript types the local binding as `number`.

options.text: Callers cannot write `<Avatar src="a.png" size={undefined} />`, because optional props reject an explicit `undefined`
options.why: Without `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `size?: number` means `number | undefined`, so an explicit `undefined` is allowed (and the default applies).

options.text: Destructuring defaults are the way to give function components default props; React 19 no longer applies `defaultProps` to function components
options.why: The React 19 upgrade guide removed `defaultProps` for function components in favour of ES6 default parameters.

options.text: Typing the component as `React.FC<{ src: string; size?: number }>` would also let it accept `children` without declaring them
options.why: `React.FC` stopped adding an implicit `children` prop in the React 18 types. You must declare `children` yourself.

options.text: The props type must be written as an `interface`; JSX attribute checking does not work with an inline object type
options.why: JSX checks attributes against any object type: inline, `type` alias or `interface`.

explanation: Optional props are marked with `?`, and defaults belong in the destructuring pattern, which also narrows the local variable to the non-`undefined` type. Interviewers use this to check that you know current React typing: no implicit `children` on `React.FC`, and no `defaultProps` for function components in React 19.

options.text: Change it to `useState<User>(null)` so the state is a `User`
options.why: Under `strictNullChecks`, `null` is not assignable to `User`, so this initial value is rejected.

options.text: Change it to `useState<User | null>(null)` so the state can hold either
options.why: The type argument describes every value the state will hold. `useState(null)` alone infers the type `null`, so no `User` can ever be stored.

options.text: Keep `useState(null)` and write `setUser(u as null)`
options.why: This silences the error by lying about the value. `user` stays typed as `null`, so reading `user.name` would still fail to type-check.

options.text: Change it to `useState<any>(null)` because the user arrives asynchronously
options.why: It compiles, but it switches off checking for every use of `user`, which is the opposite of what the interviewer wants.

explanation: `useState` infers its type from the initial value, and `useState(null)` infers `null`. When the initial value is a placeholder, write the full type: `useState<User | null>(null)`. Consumers then have to handle `null` before rendering, which is the point.

stem: Which statements about `useRef` are true with React 19 and its current `@types/react` under `strict`? (Choose two.)

options.text: `const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)` has type `RefObject<HTMLInputElement | null>`, so you call `inputRef.current?.focus()`
options.why: The `null` overload adds `| null` to `current`, which matches the time before the element is mounted.

options.text: `useRef<number>()` with no argument is a compile error; you write `useRef<number | null>(null)` or pass an initial value
options.why: React 19's types made the argument required, so every `useRef` call must pass an initial value.

options.text: `inputRef.current.focus()` compiles inside a click handler, because the compiler knows the ref is set after mount
options.why: The compiler has no idea when React attaches the ref. `current` is still `HTMLInputElement | null`, so this is a "possibly null" error.

options.text: A DOM ref must be created with `React.MutableRefObject` or it cannot be passed to the `ref` attribute
options.why: React 19 uses a single mutable `RefObject` type, and `MutableRefObject` is deprecated. `useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)` can be passed to `ref` directly.

options.text: The `current` property of a DOM ref is `readonly` in React 19, so `timerRef.current = id` needs a separate hook
options.why: In React 19's types `RefObject.current` is mutable, so the same `useRef` can hold DOM nodes and mutable values such as timer ids.

explanation: For DOM refs, pass the element type and `null`: `useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)`. Then access `current` with optional chaining or a null check. React 19 requires an argument for `useRef` and treats every ref as mutable. Interviewers probe whether you know refs are empty until React attaches them.

options.text: `type Action = { type: string; amount?: number };`
options.why: Any string is a valid `type`, so typos compile. `amount` is optional everywhere, so a missing amount compiles too.

options.text: `type Action = { type: "increment" | "add" | "reset"; amount?: number };`
options.why: This catches typos, but `amount` is still optional for every action, so `{ type: "add" }` compiles.

options.text: `type Action = { type: "increment" } | { type: "add"; amount: number } | { type: "reset" };`
options.why: A discriminated union ties each `type` to its own payload, so `"add"` requires `amount` and unknown `type` strings are rejected.

options.text: `type Action = Record<string, unknown>;`
options.why: Any object is accepted, and inside the reducer every field is `unknown`. No mistakes are caught at the call site.

explanation: Type reducer actions as a discriminated union on `type`. `dispatch` is inferred from the reducer, so each call is checked against the exact action shapes, and the reducer's `switch` narrows `action` so that `action.amount` is a `number` in the `"add"` case.

options.text: `Event`
options.why: That is the DOM `Event` type, not React's synthetic event. React's `onChange` prop rejects a handler that expects a DOM `Event`.

options.text: `React.MouseEvent<HTMLInputElement, MouseEvent>`
options.why: A mouse event type does not match `onChange`, which passes a `ChangeEvent`. The handler is rejected.

options.text: `React.ChangeEvent<HTMLElement>`
options.why: The prop accepts this handler, but `e.target` is then an `HTMLElement`, which has no `value`, so `e.target.value` fails.

options.text: `React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>`
options.why: This is the event type `onChange` passes for an `<input>`. Its `target` is typed as the input, so `value` is a `string`.

explanation: React handlers receive React's synthetic event types, which are generic over the element: `React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>`, `React.MouseEvent<HTMLButtonElement>` and so on. A quick trick in interviews: write the handler inline first, hover the parameter to see the inferred type, then extract it.

options.text: `React.SubmitEvent<HTMLFormElement>`
options.why: Recent `@types/react` types `onSubmit` with React's own `SubmitEvent`, so this matches exactly.

options.text: `React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>`
options.why: It still compiles, because `FormEvent` is structurally a plain synthetic event. Newer `@types/react` marks it deprecated in favour of `SubmitEvent` or `ChangeEvent`.

options.text: `SubmitEvent` with no `React.` prefix
options.why: Without the namespace this is the DOM's global `SubmitEvent`, not React's synthetic event, and the prop rejects it.

options.text: `React.MouseEvent<HTMLFormElement>`
options.why: A submit is not a mouse event. The mouse-specific properties are missing from the submit event, so the handler is rejected.

options.text: `Event`
options.why: This is the DOM `Event` type. React passes its own synthetic event, which is not assignable to the DOM type.

explanation: Most tutorials and interview answers use `React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>`, and it still works. Newer `@types/react` adds `React.SubmitEvent` (and deprecates `FormEvent`) to match the event React actually passes. The real trap is forgetting the `React.` prefix and getting the DOM's global `SubmitEvent` or `Event` instead.

stem: A reviewer asks when you need to annotate React event handler parameters. Which statements are true under `strict`? (Choose two.)

options.text: An inline handler such as `onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)}` needs no annotation; `e` is contextually typed from the `onChange` prop
options.why: The prop's type flows into the arrow function, so `e` is `React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>` for an `<input>`.

options.text: A handler declared on its own, such as `const onChange = (e) => ...`, is inferred from the JSX element it is later passed to
options.why: Inference does not flow backwards from a later use. The parameter is implicitly `any`, which `strict` reports as an error.

options.text: A handler declared on its own can be typed as a whole, for example `const onChange: React.ChangeEventHandler<HTMLInputElement> = (e) => ...`
options.why: Annotating the variable with a handler type gives the arrow function a contextual type, so `e` needs no separate annotation.

options.text: Typing `e` as `any` is recommended, because synthetic events do not match any DOM type
options.why: React ships precise synthetic event types. `any` throws away the checks on `e.target` and `e.currentTarget`.

options.text: `React.MouseEvent` and `React.ChangeEvent` are interchangeable, because both extend the synthetic event base type
options.why: They share a base, but each prop expects its own event type. A `MouseEvent` handler is rejected by `onChange`.

explanation: Inline handlers are typed for free by contextual typing. Once a handler is pulled out into a variable, annotate either the parameter (`e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>`) or the whole function (`React.ChangeEventHandler<HTMLInputElement>`). Interviewers ask this to see whether you understand where the types come from.

stem: A `Layout` component wraps whatever its parent passes: text, numbers, one or more elements, or nothing conditionally (`{isAdmin && <AdminBar />}`). Which `children` type accepts all of these?

options.text: `children: React.JSX.Element`
options.why: That is a single element only. Text, numbers, `false`, `null` and several sibling elements are all rejected.

options.text: `children: React.ReactNode`
options.why: `ReactNode` is the union of everything React can render: elements, strings, numbers, booleans, `null`, `undefined` and arrays of these.

options.text: `children: React.ReactElement[]`
options.why: Only arrays of elements are allowed. A single child, plain text and `null` are all rejected.

options.text: `children: string | React.ReactElement`
options.why: This misses numbers, `null`, `false` from `&&`, and several children (which arrive as an array).

explanation: `React.ReactNode` is the standard type for `children` that can be anything renderable. Narrower types such as `React.JSX.Element` only fit when you really require exactly one element, for example when you clone it.

options.text: `{ title: string } & { children: React.ReactNode }`, so every caller must pass children
options.why: The `children` that `PropsWithChildren` adds is optional, not required.

options.text: `{ title: string } & { children?: React.JSX.Element }`, so only one element child is allowed
options.why: The added `children` is typed as `ReactNode`, which is far wider than a single element.

options.text: `{ title: string } & { children?: React.ReactNode | undefined }`
options.why:
`PropsWithChildren

` is `P & { children?: ReactNode | undefined }`: optional children of any renderable type.

options.text: `{ title: string }`, because `children` is added automatically by `React.FC`
options.why: `PropsWithChildren` itself adds `children`. And `React.FC` has not added implicit `children` since the React 18 types.

explanation: `PropsWithChildren` is a helper that adds an optional `children?: ReactNode`. If children are required, or must be a narrower type, declare `children` yourself instead. Interviewers like this because many people still believe `React.FC` adds `children` for you.

options.text:
`

Hi

`
options.why: Exactly one element child matches `React.JSX.Element`.

options.text: `<Card>Hello {name}</Card>`
options.why: Text plus an expression become an array of children, and strings are not `JSX.Element`s.

options.text: `<Card>{isWide ? <Wide /> : <Narrow />}</Card>`
options.why: Both branches are elements, so the single child is still a `JSX.Element`.

options.text:
`

Title

Body

`
options.why: Two sibling children arrive as an array, which is not assignable to a single `JSX.Element`.

options.text: `<Card>{null}</Card>`
options.why: `null` is a valid React node, but it is not a `JSX.Element`, so it is rejected.

explanation: `React.JSX.Element` means exactly one element. Text, `null` and multiple siblings all fail. That restriction is sometimes intended, but it is usually a bug for a wrapper component, and `React.ReactNode` is the right choice. Interviewers use this to check that you know what JSX children compile to.

options.text: `useCallback` returns `unknown` unless you pass a type argument
options.why: `useCallback` keeps the type of the function you give it, here `() => void`.

options.text: The return type is `(boolean | (() => void))[]`, so `toggleOpen` might be a `boolean`
options.why: An array literal is inferred as an array of the union of its elements, not as a tuple, so each destructured item has the union type.

options.text: Hooks cannot return arrays; only `useState` is allowed to return a tuple
options.why: Custom hooks can return anything. The problem is only how TypeScript infers the array literal.

options.text: `toggleOpen` is `undefined` at runtime, because a custom hook's return value is not memoized between renders
options.why: The value exists at runtime. This is a compile-time error about the inferred type, not a runtime problem.

explanation: TypeScript infers `[a, b]` as an array of `A | B`, not as the tuple `[A, B]`, so positions lose their individual types. A custom hook that returns a `useState`-style pair needs `as const` or an explicit tuple return type. This is the classic custom-hook typing question.

stem: Following on from a `useToggle` hook that ends with `return [on, toggle];`, which changes let callers write `const [open, toggle] = useToggle(); toggle();` with `open: boolean`? (Choose two.)

options.text: End the hook with `return [on, toggle] as const;`
options.why: `as const` infers the readonly tuple `readonly [boolean, () => void]`, so each position keeps its own type.

options.text: Annotate the hook's return type as `[boolean, () => void]`
options.why: An explicit tuple return type gives the array literal a tuple context and documents the API.

options.text: End the hook with `return [on, toggle] as Array<boolean | (() => void)>;`
options.why: That is the same union array that caused the problem. `toggle` would still not be callable.

options.text: Call `useState<[boolean, () => void]>(initial)` inside the hook
options.why: That types the state itself as a tuple, which is wrong and does not compile with a `boolean` initial value.

options.text: Mark the hook with `useCallback` so React preserves the tuple type
options.why: `useCallback` memoizes a function. It has no effect on how the returned array literal is typed.

explanation: Either `as const` or an explicit tuple return type turns the result into a tuple. `as const` also makes it `readonly`, which is harmless for destructuring. Returning an object (`{ on, toggle }`) is the other common answer once a hook returns more than two values.

stem:
Write the props for a reusable `List` so that `renderItem` and `getKey` are typed from whatever `items` contains:

```tsx
<List items={users} renderItem={(u) => u.name} getKey={(u) => u.id} />
// u should be User, and u.email should be an error if User has no email
```

Which definition does that?

options.why: With `any`, `u` is `any`, so `u.email` compiles and nothing ties the callbacks to the items.
`T` is inferred from `items` at each use, so the callbacks receive `User` and misspelled properties are errors.
`u` is `object`, so even `u.name` is an error. The element type of `items` is lost.
`T` is declared but the callbacks take `unknown`, so `u.name` does not compile without a cast.

explanation: A generic component is a generic function: declare a type parameter, use it in the props, and TypeScript infers it from the JSX attributes. You can also pass it explicitly as `<List<User> ... />`. The interviewer is checking that the type flows from the data into the callbacks.

stem:
In a `.tsx` file, this line fails with "JSX element 'T' has no corresponding closing tag":

```tsx
const List = <T>(props: ListProps<T>) => { /* ... */ };
```

Which declarations give you a working generic component in the same `.tsx` file? (Choose three.)

options.text: `const List = <T,>(props: ListProps<T>) => { /* ... */ };`
options.why: The trailing comma tells the parser this is a type parameter list, not a JSX tag.

options.text: `const List = <T extends unknown>(props: ListProps<T>) => { /* ... */ };`
options.why: An `extends` clause also removes the ambiguity with a JSX opening tag.

options.text: `function List<T>(props: ListProps<T>) { /* ... */ }`
options.why: Function declarations have no JSX ambiguity, so plain `<T>` works there.

options.text: `const List: React.FC<ListProps<T>> = (props) => { /* ... */ };`
options.why: `T` is not declared anywhere, so this is "Cannot find name 'T'". `React.FC` cannot introduce a type parameter for you.

options.text: Add `"jsx": "preserve"` to `tsconfig.json` so `<T>` is no longer parsed as JSX
options.why: The `jsx` option controls output, not parsing. Any `.tsx` file parses `<T>(...) =>` as JSX.

explanation: In `.tsx`, `<T>` at the start of an arrow function looks like a JSX tag. Use `<T,>`, `<T extends unknown>`, or a function declaration. This catches out many candidates who have only written generics in `.ts` files.

options.text: It compiles, and `u` is inferred as `User` from `items`
options.why: `T` is fixed to `unknown` by the annotation, so there is nothing left to infer from `items`.

options.text: `u` is `unknown`, so `u.name` is a compile error
options.why: `React.FC<ListProps<unknown>>` is not generic. Every caller gets `unknown`, and the component has to be a generic function to infer `User`.

options.text: `u` is `any`, so it compiles but nothing is checked
options.why: That would happen with `ListProps<any>`. Here it is `unknown`, which blocks property access.

options.text: The annotation itself fails, because `React.FC` cannot take a generic props type
options.why: `React.FC` accepts any props type. The annotation is valid; it just fixes `T` to one type.

explanation:
`React.FC

` describes one concrete props type. It cannot express "for any `T`", so generic components are written as generic functions (`function List(...)` or `(...) =>`). Pick `unknown` and callers lose the types; pick `any` and they lose the checks.

stem:
An auth context has no sensible default. Consumers should get an `Auth` value (never `null`), and using the context outside the provider should fail loudly. Which implementation does that?

```tsx
type Auth = { user: User; logout: () => void };
```

options.why: This compiles, but outside a provider consumers get `{}` typed as `Auth`, so the failure shows up later as `undefined` fields.
The `!` hides `null` from the type but not at runtime. Outside a provider this returns `null`, and the crash happens wherever it is first used.
The null check narrows `ctx` to `Auth`, so consumers never see `null`, and missing providers fail immediately with a clear message.
It is type-safe, but every consumer has to handle `null`, which is exactly the noise the interviewer asked you to remove.

explanation: The common pattern is: create the context with `T | null`, then expose a custom hook that checks for `null`, throws a helpful error, and returns `T`. Consumers get a clean type, and a missing provider fails at the right place instead of deep inside the UI.

options.text: A compile error, because TypeScript checks that every `useContext` call has a provider above it
options.why: TypeScript does not know the component tree. Provider placement is never checked at compile time.

options.text: React logs a "missing provider" warning in development and renders the button with no colour
options.why: React silently uses the default value. It has no idea that `{}` is not a real `Theme`.

options.text: `useContext` returns `undefined`, and the button renders without styles
options.why: With no provider, `useContext` returns the default value passed to `createContext`, here `{}`, not `undefined`.

options.text: It throws a `TypeError` while rendering, because `theme.colors` is `undefined`
options.why: The default `{}` was asserted to be a `Theme`, so the compiler trusts `theme.colors`, but at runtime it does not exist.

explanation: `{} as Theme` is a type assertion that lies to the compiler. It is a common shortcut that turns a missing provider into a confusing runtime crash. Either supply a real default value or use `Theme | null` with a checking hook.

stem: Which statements about typing context are true with React 19 and its current `@types/react`? (Choose two.)

options.text: `createContext<string>()` with no argument is a compile error; a default value is always required
options.why: The type definition requires `defaultValue`. You pass `null` (typed as `T | null`) when there is no sensible default.

options.text: You can render the context itself as a provider, such as `<AuthContext value={auth}>`, and its `value` is checked against the context's type
options.why: React 19 lets the context object act as a provider, and the types check `value` against `T`.

options.text: `<AuthContext.Provider>` no longer type-checks in React 19 and must be migrated before upgrading
options.why: `Context.Provider` still works and is still typed. React plans to deprecate it later.

options.text: `useContext(ctx)` automatically returns `T | undefined` so that a missing provider is visible in the type
options.why: `useContext` returns `T`. Without a provider it returns the default value, so the type only includes `null` if you put it there.

options.text: If a provider passes `value={undefined}`, consumers fall back to the default value from `createContext`
options.why: The default is only used when there is no provider above. A provider with `value={undefined}` provides `undefined`.

explanation: The context type comes from `createContext<T>(defaultValue)`, and `useContext` simply returns `T`. To make a missing provider visible, put `null` in `T` and wrap the read in a checking hook. React 19 also lets you render `<Ctx value={...}>` directly.

stem: A team's style guide says "props use `interface`". Which of these props types cannot be written as a single `interface`, so it needs a `type` alias?

options.text: Props that extend the native button attributes, written as `ComponentProps<"button">` plus a `variant: "primary" | "ghost"` prop
options.why: `interface ButtonProps extends ComponentProps<"button"> { variant: ... }` works. An interface can extend an object type alias.

options.text: Props with an optional callback: `{ onClose?: () => void }`
options.why: Optional members and function types are ordinary interface members.

options.text: Props that are one of two shapes: `{ kind: "info"; message: string } | { kind: "error"; message: string; retry: () => void }`
options.why: A union of shapes is not an object type, and an interface can only describe a single object type.

options.text: Props where one property is a union: `{ size: "sm" | "md" | "lg" }`
options.why: Union-typed properties are fine inside an interface. Only a union of whole prop objects needs a type alias.

explanation: For plain object props, `interface` and `type` are interchangeable, so consistency matters more than the choice. A `type` alias is required when props are a union (discriminated variants, mutually exclusive props) or are computed with mapped or conditional types.

stem: An interviewer asks: "`interface` or `type` for React props, and does it matter?" Which statements would be accurate parts of your answer? (Choose two.)

options.text: For an ordinary object of props, both work the same in JSX checking, so pick one convention and stay consistent
options.why: JSX checks attributes structurally against any object type, however it was declared.

options.text: `interface Props extends ComponentProps<"input"> { onChange: (v: string) => void }` reports the conflicting `onChange` at the declaration, while `ComponentProps<"input"> & { onChange: ... }` combines the two types without any error
options.why: Interface `extends` checks member compatibility; an intersection just merges members, which for conflicting primitives silently gives `never`.

options.text: Only interfaces can be used as the props of a generic component
options.why: Generic type aliases (`type ListProps<T> = ...`) work just as well.

options.text: Type aliases are not supported by `React.FC`
options.why:
`React.FC

` accepts any object type for `P`, including aliases.

options.text: Interfaces can describe a union of prop shapes if you list each shape as a separate `extends`
options.why: Extending several interfaces combines them into one object type (all members), which is the opposite of a union.

explanation: The honest answer is "mostly no": both work for object props. The real differences are that only `type` can express unions and computed types, interfaces can be merged and extended with conflict checking, and intersections can hide conflicts. Interviewers want those trade-offs, not a strong opinion.

stem: A `Tooltip` has a `content` prop that callers fill with a plain string, a number, an element such as `Pro`, or `null` to show nothing. Which type should `content` have?

options.text: `React.JSX.Element`
options.why: That only accepts a single element. Strings, numbers and `null` are rejected.

options.text: `React.ReactElement`
options.why: A `ReactElement` is an element object. Strings, numbers and `null` are not elements.

options.text: `React.ReactNode`
options.why: `ReactNode` is everything React can render, including strings, numbers, elements, `null` and `undefined`.

options.text: `string | React.JSX.Element`
options.why: Numbers and `null` are still rejected, so this is too narrow for the stated uses.

explanation: Use `React.ReactNode` for any prop that is rendered as content. `React.ReactElement` and `React.JSX.Element` are for when you need an actual element object, for example to clone it or read its props.

stem: Which statements about `React.JSX.Element`, `React.ReactElement` and `React.ReactNode` are true with TypeScript 5.1+ and React 19's types? (Choose two.)

options.text: `React.JSX.Element` is a `ReactElement<any, any>`: the object a JSX expression produces, so strings and `null` are not assignable to it
options.why: It is an alias for an element object, which is why it is too narrow for `children` or content props.

options.text: `React.ReactNode` includes `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, elements, and iterables of nodes
options.why: That union is what React can render, which is why it is the type for `children`.

options.text: A component annotated `function Empty(): React.JSX.Element` may `return null`
options.why: `null` is not a `JSX.Element`, so the annotation rejects it. Use `React.ReactNode` as the return type, or let it be inferred.

options.text: `function Hello() { return "hi"; }` cannot be used as `<Hello />`, because components must return an element
options.why: Since TypeScript 5.1 and the React 18 types, a component may return any `ReactNode`, including a string.

options.text: In React 19's types the global `JSX.Element` is the recommended spelling and `React.JSX` is deprecated
options.why: It is the other way round: React 19's types removed the global `JSX` namespace. Use `React.JSX.Element`.

explanation: `ReactNode` is the wide "anything renderable" type, and `ReactElement` / `React.JSX.Element` are element objects only. Modern TypeScript lets components return any `ReactNode`, so annotating return types as `JSX.Element` mostly creates errors. In React 19, use the `React.JSX` namespace rather than the global `JSX`.

options.text: Make `address` optional (`address?: ...`) so the compiler forces `user.address?.city` or a check
options.why: Once the type admits the missing case, `user.address.city` becomes a "possibly undefined" error until you handle it.

options.text: Add `user.address!.city`, telling TypeScript the address is always present
options.why: This asserts the bug away. The compiler stops checking and the crash still happens.

options.text: Wrap the component in a React error boundary, so that a missing address can no longer crash the whole page
options.why: An error boundary contains the crash at runtime. The types still say the address always exists, so the compiler still cannot help.

options.text: Change `user: User` to `user: any` while the API is unstable
options.why: This removes all checking, so the same mistake goes unnoticed everywhere.

explanation: Types only help if they describe the real data. If the API can omit a field, mark it optional, and `strictNullChecks` then forces every read to handle the missing case. The interviewer wants to hear that the type was wrong, not that the component needs a try/catch.

stem:
Under `strict`, which line is a compile error? ```tsx type User = { name: string }; function Profile() { const [user, setUser] = useState(); // line 1 useEffect(() => { loadUser().then(setUser); }, []); // line 2 const title = user.name.toUpperCase(); // line 3 if (!user) return

Loading...

; // line 4 return

{user.name}

; // line 5 } ```

options.text: Line 1: `useState<User>()` needs an initial value
options.why: `useState` with no argument is allowed and gives a state of type `User | undefined`.

options.text: Line 3: `user` is `User | undefined`, so `user.name` is "possibly undefined"
options.why: Line 3 reads the state before the loading check, when `user` may still be `undefined`.

options.text: Line 5: `user` may still be `undefined` inside the returned JSX, because narrowing does not reach JSX
options.why: The early return on line 4 narrows `user` to `User` for the rest of the function.

options.text: Line 2: `setUser` cannot be passed directly to `then`
options.why: `setUser` accepts a `User`, which is what `loadUser()` resolves with, so passing it directly is fine.

explanation: `useState<User>()` with no initial value is typed `User | undefined`, so the compiler forces you to handle the loading state before reading fields. Moving line 3 below the guard fixes it. This is exactly how types prevent the "undefined API data" crash.

stem: Implement `useBoolean(initial?)` returning `value` plus `setTrue`, `setFalse` and `toggle`. Callers should be able to call each function with full type safety, and the functions should be stable between renders. Which implementation is correct?

options.why: The array literal is inferred as `(boolean | (() => void))[]`, so a destructured `setTrue()` is a compile error. The functions are also recreated every render.
The return type is inferred as `{ value: boolean; setTrue: () => void; ... }`, and the functional updater lets `toggle` be stable with empty dependencies.
It type-checks, but `toggle` closes over the first render's `value` because of the empty dependency list, so it always sets `!initial`.
The annotation widens every property to `boolean | (() => void)`, so `toggle()` does not compile, and typos like `b.togle` are allowed.

explanation: Small hooks are a common warm-up. The interviewer checks that the return type is precise (an object, or a tuple with `as const`), that you do not annotate it more loosely than inference would, and that stable callbacks use the functional state updater instead of a stale value.

stem: Implement `useDefault(defaultValue, initialValue?)`: it behaves like `useState`, but whenever the state is `null` or `undefined` it returns `defaultValue` instead. The returned value must be typed as `T` (never `null` or `undefined`), and valid values such as `0` or `""` must be kept. Which implementation is correct?

options.why: `??` only falls back on `null` or `undefined`, so `0` and `""` survive, and `value ?? defaultValue` is typed `T`.
`||` also replaces `0`, `""` and `false` with the default, which breaks the requirement to keep valid falsy values.
The default is never applied, and callers get `T | null | undefined` instead of `T`.
It types as `T`, but the default only applies to the first render. A later `setValue(null)` does not compile, so the state can never be reset to the default.

explanation: Keep the state type wide (`T | null | undefined`) so callers can clear it, and narrow the returned value with `??`, which TypeScript understands removes `null` and `undefined`. Mixing up `||` and `??` is the bug interviewers are looking for here.

stem: In a code review of a React + TypeScript codebase, which of these are real mistakes? (Choose three.)

options.text: `const [tags, setTags] = useState([]);` for a list of strings
options.why: The state is inferred as `never[]`, so adding any string is a compile error. Write `useState<string[]>([])`.

options.text: `useEffect(async () => { const data = await load(); setData(data); }, []);`
options.why: An async function returns a promise, and an effect must return nothing or a cleanup function. The types reject it; call an inner async function instead.

options.text: `function Panel({ children }: { children: React.JSX.Element })` for a wrapper that receives text and several elements
options.why: `React.JSX.Element` accepts exactly one element. A general wrapper should use `React.ReactNode`.

options.text: `const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);` for a ref passed to `<input ref={inputRef} />`
options.why: This is the recommended way to type a DOM ref in React 19.

options.text: `const [count, setCount] = useState(0);` with no type argument
options.why: The initial value already describes the full type, so inferring `number` is correct and idiomatic.

options.text: `onChange={(e) => setQuery(e.target.value)}` with no annotation on `e`
options.why: Inline handlers are contextually typed from the prop, so `e` is already a `ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>`.

explanation: Most React + TypeScript mistakes come from types that do not match what React does: empty initial state inferring `never[]`, async effect callbacks, and children typed too narrowly. Interviewers also want you to recognise where inference is already correct, so you do not over-annotate.

options.text: `useEffect` callbacks must be typed with `React.EffectCallback`; add that annotation
options.why: The callback is already checked against `EffectCallback`. That check is what fails, so annotating it does not help.

options.text: The callback returns a `Promise`, but an effect may only return nothing or a cleanup function; define an async function inside the effect and call it
options.why: `() => Promise<void>` is not assignable to `() => void | Destructor`. An inner async function keeps the effect itself synchronous.

options.text: `await` is not allowed in the body of a component; move the fetch into an event handler
options.why: `await` is fine inside any async function, including one declared inside an effect.

options.text: `res.json()` returns `any`, so `setUser` rejects it
options.why: `any` is assignable to the setter's parameter type. That part compiles (unsafely).

explanation: React uses the effect's return value as its cleanup function, so the types only allow `void` or a function. Declare `async function load() { ... }` inside the effect, call it, and use a flag or `AbortController` in the cleanup to ignore stale responses.

options.text: Switch to `type TextFieldProps = React.ComponentProps<"input"> & { onChange: (value: string) => void }` so the two are merged
options.why: The intersection hides the error, but `onChange` becomes both signatures at once, so the conflict is still there in a confusing form.

options.text: Keep the interface and add `// @ts-expect-error` above the `onChange` line
options.why: That silences the check without fixing the conflicting type, so the component and its callers still disagree.

options.text: Use `interface TextFieldProps extends Omit<React.ComponentProps<"input">, "onChange"> { onChange: (value: string) => void }`
options.why: Removing the native `onChange` first lets you redefine it with your own signature, with no conflict.

options.text: Rename the prop to `onchange` so it does not clash with the native one
options.why: This avoids the clash with a confusing name, and the native `onChange` is still accepted with the event signature.

explanation: When a wrapper changes the meaning of a native prop, `Omit` the native one and declare your own. Interface `extends` usefully reports the conflict, while an intersection would quietly combine the two. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can extend DOM props safely.

stem: You are building a small `useQuery` hook. Consumers should only be able to read `data` after checking that the request succeeded, and only read `error` after checking that it failed. Which state type does that?

options.text: `type QueryState<T> = { loading: boolean; error?: Error; data?: T };`
options.why: Every field is always available. After checking `!loading && !error`, `data` is still `T | undefined`, and impossible combinations like loading-with-error are allowed.

options.text: `type QueryState<T> = { status: "loading" | "error" | "success"; data: T | null; error: Error | null };`
options.why: Checking `status` does not narrow `data` or `error`, because they are not tied to a specific status.

options.text: `type QueryState<T> = [T | undefined, Error | undefined, boolean];`
options.why: A tuple has the same problem as the loose object: checking one slot says nothing to the compiler about the others.

options.text: `type QueryState<T> = { status: "loading" } | { status: "error"; error: Error } | { status: "success"; data: T };`
options.why: A discriminated union means `data` only exists in the success branch, so the compiler forces the status check before it is read.

explanation: Model fetch state as a discriminated union on `status`. Each branch carries only the fields that make sense, impossible states cannot be built, and `switch (q.status)` narrows correctly. This is what the interviewer is looking for in a "typed useFetch" machine-coding round.

options.text: Line 1, because `T` cannot be inferred from a callback's return type
options.why: `T` is inferred from the callback's return type `Promise<{ name: string }>`, so `T` is `{ name: string }`.

options.text: Line 4, because `q` could still be `"success"` there
options.why: After the `"loading"` return, `q` is the error or success member, and the `=== "error"` check narrows it to the error member.

options.text: Line 5, because `q.data` may be `undefined`
options.why: By line 5 the loading and error members have been ruled out, so `q` is the success member and `data` is present.

options.text: Line 2, because `data` is not on every member of the union
options.why: Before any check, `q` may be loading or error, and those members have no `data` property.

explanation: With a discriminated union you can only touch branch-specific fields after narrowing on the discriminant. Early returns narrow the rest of the function. Inferring `T` from the fetcher's `Promise<T>` saves callers from writing type arguments.

stem: Callers should write `useQuery(() => fetchUser(id))` with no type arguments and get `QueryState<User>` back, where `fetchUser` returns `Promise<User>`. Which signature does that?

options.text: `function useQuery<T>(url: string): QueryState<T>`
options.why: Nothing in the arguments mentions `T`, so it cannot be inferred and defaults to `unknown`. It also takes a URL, not a fetcher.

options.text: `function useQuery<T>(fetcher: () => T): QueryState<T>`
options.why: `T` is inferred as `Promise<User>`, so `data` would be typed as a promise rather than the user.

options.text: `function useQuery<T>(fetcher: () => Promise<T>): QueryState<T>`
options.why: Matching `Promise<User>` against `Promise<T>` infers `T` as `User`, so `data` is a `User`.

options.text: `function useQuery(fetcher: () => Promise<unknown>): QueryState<unknown>`
options.why: It accepts the call, but every consumer gets `unknown` data and has to cast.

explanation: Put the type parameter where TypeScript can see it in the arguments, and shape the parameter (`() => Promise<T>`) so that inference unwraps the promise. A generic used only in the return type, like `useQuery<T>(url)`, is just a hidden cast.

stem: Implement a typed `cn(...args)` (like the `classnames` package). It must accept strings, falsy values from conditions such as `isActive && "active"`, objects such as `{ disabled: isDisabled }`, and arrays nested to any depth. Which argument type does that?

options.text:
```ts
type ClassValue = string | Record<string, boolean>
  | Array<string | Record<string, boolean>>;
```
options.why: This accepts only one level of array, and it rejects the `false` produced by `isActive && "active"`.
This accepts the right inputs, but also any object, function or array of anything, so mistakes are not caught.
Objects, arrays and the `false` from a condition are all rejected.
The falsy members cover conditional strings, `ClassDict` covers object syntax, and the recursive `ClassValue[]` covers arrays at any depth.

explanation: A recursive type alias (`ClassValue[]` inside `ClassValue`) describes arbitrarily nested arrays. Including the falsy types lets callers write `cond && "cls"` directly. Interviewers use this to test recursive types and the difference between a precise union and `object`.

options.text: `cn("btn", isOn && "btn-on")`
options.why: `isOn && "btn-on"` is `false | "btn-on"`, and both members are in `ClassValue`.

options.text: `cn({ active: 1 })`
options.why: Object values must be `boolean`, `null` or `undefined`. A number is rejected.
The recursive `ClassValue[]` accepts arrays nested inside arrays, including objects inside them.

options.text: `cn(isOn)`
options.why: `isOn` is `boolean`, which includes `true`. Only `false` is in the union, so a bare boolean is rejected.

options.text: `cn(maybe, null)`
options.why: `string | undefined` and `null` are both part of `ClassValue`.

explanation: Including `false` but not `true` is a deliberate design choice: `cond && "cls"` type-checks, while a bare boolean (almost always a bug) does not. The `ClassDict` value type keeps object syntax honest.

stem: Design the props for a `Button` that renders a link when given `href` and a button when given `onClick`. Passing both, or neither, must be a compile error. Which props type does that?

options.text:
```tsx
type ButtonProps = { children: React.ReactNode } &
  ({ href: string } | { onClick: () => void });
```
options.why: Excess property checks accept a property if any member of the union has it, so `href` plus `onClick` together compiles.

options.text:
```tsx
type ButtonProps = { children: React.ReactNode } &
  Partial<{ href: string; onClick: () => void }>;
```
options.why: Both props are optional and independent, so both and neither are allowed.

options.text:
```tsx
type ButtonProps = { children: React.ReactNode } &
  ({ href: string; onClick?: never } | { onClick: () => void; href?: never });
```
options.why: Each member forbids the other prop with `?: never`, so both together match neither member, and neither prop matches neither member.
This requires both props, which is the opposite of mutually exclusive.

explanation: A plain union is not exclusive in TypeScript, because object types are open. Adding `otherProp?: never` to each member makes the shapes exclusive. This is the pattern senior candidates are expected to reach for when asked to make invalid prop combinations impossible.

options.text: `<Button href="/pricing">Pricing</Button>`
options.why: This matches `LinkProps`; `onClick` is simply absent.

options.text: `<Button href="/pricing" onClick={f}>Pricing</Button>`
options.why: `onClick: () => void` is not assignable to `never` in `LinkProps`, and `href` is not assignable to `never` in `ActionProps`.

options.text: `<Button>Pricing</Button>`
options.why: Neither member matches: `LinkProps` needs `href` and `ActionProps` needs `onClick`.

options.text: `<Button href="/pricing" onClick={undefined}>Pricing</Button>`
options.why: `onClick?: never` means `undefined` is allowed when `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is off, so this matches `LinkProps`.

options.text: `<Button onClick={f}>Buy</Button>`
options.why: This matches `ActionProps`; `href` is simply absent.

explanation: `prop?: never` really means "absent or `undefined`", so passing `undefined` explicitly is allowed unless `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is on. The union still catches the real mistakes: both props, or neither. Inside the component, checking `props.href !== undefined` narrows `props` to one member.

stem:
A teammate's first attempt at exclusive props compiles a call they expected to fail:

```tsx
type Props = { children: React.ReactNode } & ({ href: string } | { onClick: () => void });
declare function Button(props: Props): React.ReactNode;

<Button href="/x" onClick={() => {}}>Go</Button>; // no error
```

Why is there no error?

options.text: JSX attributes are not checked for excess properties at all, unlike object literals
options.why: JSX attributes do get excess property checks; `<Button foo="x">` would be an error here.

options.text: The intersection with `{ children: React.ReactNode }` collapses the union into a single object type in which both props become optional
options.why: Intersecting with an object distributes over the union; it does not merge the members or make props optional.

options.text: For a union target, a property only counts as excess if no member of the union declares it, and both `href` and `onClick` are declared by some member
options.why: The value matches the `href` member structurally, and the extra `onClick` is known to the other member, so it is not flagged.

options.text: Union types in props are checked only against the first member, which accepts the call
options.why: TypeScript checks against all members. The issue is that extra properties are allowed when another member declares them.

explanation: Object types are open: a value with extra properties still matches. Excess property checking is a narrower lint for fresh object literals, and for unions it only flags properties no member knows about. That is why exclusive props need `?: never` (or a discriminant) on each member.

options.text: `as const satisfies Record<Variant, string>`
options.why: `satisfies` checks that every variant has a string, and `as const` keeps each value as its literal type.

options.text: Nothing; annotate the variable instead: `const styles: Record<Variant, string> = { ... }`
options.why: This catches a missing variant, but the annotation becomes the type, so `styles.primary` is widened to `string`.

options.text: `as Record<Variant, string>`
options.why: An assertion does not report missing keys (the types only need to be comparable), and the values are widened to `string`.

options.text: `as const`
options.why: This keeps the literals, but nothing compares the keys with `Variant`, so a new variant goes unnoticed.

explanation: `satisfies` validates a value against a type without replacing the value's inferred type, and `as const` keeps literal values. Together they give exhaustive coverage of the variant union plus precise derived types, which is the behaviour design-system maintainers want when a variant is added.
